title: Split It: the Break-Apart Trick for 6, 7, 8

steps.body: The stubborn facts — 6s, 7s, 8s — crack open with one move: **split a hard number into friendly pieces**. 7 × 6: split the 6 into 5 + 1, so 7 × 6 = 7 × 5 + 7 × 1 = 35 + 7 = 42. It's an array cut into two smaller arrays.
Cut one array into two easier rectangles.

widget.prompt: Split the 8-by-7 array into an 8-by-5 rectangle and an 8-by-2 rectangle. Use the shown pieces to choose the whole product.

choices.label: 56 squares
choices.feedback: Yes. The two pieces cover 40 + 16 = 56 squares.

choices.label: 40 squares
choices.feedback: That counts only the 8-by-5 piece. Add the 8-by-2 piece too.

choices.label: 15 squares
choices.feedback: Adding the factors does not count the squares. Find each rectangle's area, then add.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The pieces contain 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16 squares. Add them.
widget.successFeedback: The pieces rebuild all 56 squares. Splitting 8 × 7 into 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 changes the work, not the answer.

predict.prompt: 8 × 7 split into 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 — does splitting change the answer?

options.label: It only works for even numbers

predict.reveal: Cutting the 7 into 5 + 2 just slices the array down the middle: 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16 rebuild the whole 56. Break-apart works because the two pieces still cover every row.

steps.body: A legal split keeps one factor whole and cuts the other into pieces that **rebuild it**.
explanationVariants: 5 + 2 rebuilds the 7, and the 6 rides along in both pieces: 6 × 5 + 6 × 2 = 30 + 12 = 42.
Picture the 6-by-7 array with a cut after column 5: a 6 × 5 block and a 6 × 2 block.

options.feedback: 5 + 2 rebuilds the 7, and both pieces keep the 6: 30 + 12 = 42.
The 2 forgot its six! Cutting the array leaves the 6 in BOTH pieces — the second piece is 6 × 2, not a bare 2.
The pieces 4 + 2 rebuild 6 — but it was the 7 being cut. Your pieces must add back to 7.
That bolts a whole extra 6 × 7 onto the fives piece. The pieces come FROM the 7: like 5 and 2.

steps.body: Split rules: cut **whichever factor is friendlier to cut**, keep the other in both pieces, and make sure the pieces **add back to the original**. Best cutting spots: 5s, 2s, and 10s — the facts you now own cold.
Straight recall — split it in your head if you need to.
explanationVariants: Or split the 7: 6 × 5 + 6 × 2 = 30 + 12 = 42. Different cuts, same array.

commonErrors.feedback: 35 is the fives piece, 7 × 5 — the split's second piece (7 × 1) is still waiting to be added.
13 adds 7 + 6. Seven groups of 6 stack much higher — split the fact into 7 × 5 + 7 × 1.
76 glues the digits together. Cut the fact instead: a fives piece plus a little piece.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Split the 6 into 5 + 1: seven 5s, then seven 1s, added together.

steps.body: Splits can **subtract** too — go one group past, then give it back.

widget.prompt: Build 9 × 6 the tens way: use the ten-fact, then give back the extra group.

commonBuilds.feedback: That ADDS a group, making 11 × 6. Nine is one group LESS than ten — give the extra 6 back with −.
9 × 6 restates the question! The tens way goes THROUGH the easy fact: ten 6s, minus the one 6 you didn't need.

widget.missFeedback: Ten 6s first (10 × 6), then subtract the one extra group of 6.
widget.successFeedback: 10 × 6 − 6 = 60 − 6 = 54. Overshoot with the easy fact, then hand one group back — the nines trick is a split!

steps.body: Find the missing piece of a split.
explanationVariants: The 7 got cut into 5 + 2, so the other piece is 8 × 2: 40 + 16 = 56 plants.
Count what the fives piece misses: 8 × 5 covers 5 of each row's 7 — the last 2 in every row make 8 × 2.

widget.prompt: A garden has 8 rows of 7 plants. Kim counts it as 8 × 5 plus one more piece. Which piece?

options.feedback: 5 + 2 rebuilds the 7, with the 8 in both pieces: 40 + 16 = 56 plants.
Adding 8 × 5 again makes 8 × 10 — that rebuilds a 10, not the 7. The leftover piece is smaller.
The 7 is the number being CUT — it doesn't appear in the pieces. Every piece keeps the 8.

options.label: just 2
options.feedback: The 2 forgot its eight! Those are 2 whole plants in EVERY one of the 8 rows: 8 × 2 = 16 plants.

steps.body: A split with a sale in the middle.
hints: Careful — whole ROWS sell, not single rolls. How many rows keep their rolls?
You can split it: 7 rows of 8, minus 2 rows of 8 — or just count 5 rows of 8.
5 × 8, or 56 − 16. Both cuts of the same tray.
explanationVariants: Rows left: 7 − 2 = 5, so 5 × 8 = 40 rolls. That's the split (7 − 2) × 8.
All rolls minus sold rolls: 7 × 8 = 56, and the 2 sold rows held 2 × 8 = 16, so 56 − 16 = 40.

widget.prompt: A bakery tray holds 7 rows with 8 rolls in each row. Two full rows sell out. How many rolls are left?

commonErrors.feedback: 54 subtracts 2 ROLLS from 56 — but two whole ROWS sold, and each row held 8 rolls: give back 2 × 8 = 16.
56 is the full tray, 7 × 8 — before the sale. Two rows of 8 have left the building.
16 is what SOLD (2 rows of 8). The question asks what's LEFT — the other 5 rows.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two routes: (7 − 2) rows of 8, or the full 7 × 8 minus the sold 2 × 8. Both land on the same number.

steps.body: No fact in the table can resist you now.
takeaways: Split a hard factor into friendly pieces; the other factor rides in every piece.
The pieces must rebuild the number you cut — check by adding them.
Splits subtract too: the nines trick is 10 × n minus one group.
steps.teaser: time to use it all — the Word-Problem Workshop turns facts into answers about the real world.

concept.body: Quick rewind. To split 6 × 7, cut the 7 into **5 + 2**. Solve the two easy pieces — 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 2 = 12 — and add: 42. The 6 stays in both pieces; the cuts must add back to 7. Cut, solve, rejoin.

explanationVariants: The pieces 5 + 1 rebuild the 6, and the 4 rides in both: 20 + 4.

options.feedback: 21 added a bare 1 — the second piece keeps the 4 too: it's 4 × 1 = 4, giving 20 + 4.
20 is only the fives piece, 4 × 5. The little piece 4 × 1 still needs adding.
